name: PT Pakuwon Jati Tbk

frontmatter.title: Pakuwon Jati
frontmatter.summary: The largest listed retail landlord in Indonesia trades at a discount to asset value that we do not expect to close inside twelve months. Recurring income dominates revenue and margins; the land bank is carried at cost. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp312: the asset leg is held at the discount the market applies at the current price, so the return is the roll, the dividend and two capped market cross-checks.
thesis: A recurring-income franchise, not a housebuilder: malls, offices and hotels deliver IDR5,617.0bn of IDR7,111.1bn group revenue at segment gross margins of 56.0% blended, which is why the audited depreciation line is large and the pack’s cash-flow presentation understates EBITDA [S5].

The asset value is not in dispute, the discount is: RNAV per share before the discount is far above the Rp258 price, but we hold the 72.1% discount the market applies at that price rather than underwriting convergence, because no dated catalyst falls inside the twelve months [S2][S7].

Cross-checks are disclosed as such, not blended in as if they were scenario-tested: pe and pbv carry 5.0% each, use trailing metrics and print Rp497 and Rp489, respectively 92.5% and 89.3% above the RNAV leg — at today's multiples they would print about the share price, which is why their weight is capped [S0].

Cash-backed, conservatively financed: total cash and financial assets of IDR13,508.0bn cover the 333.4 million dollar notes several times, and the recurring rent roll covers interest by a wide margin [S2 p.28][S9 p.28].

The bear case is a real stress, not a relabelled base: it moves the cap rate, the recurring gross margin and the discount — the three inputs the RNAV actually reads — and its intrinsic value of Rp213 sits below today's price, with a rolled target of Rp231.

catalysts.event: Fourth-quarter and full-year marketing sales, the first read on whether presales have stopped falling [S4]
Fiscal decision on the PPN DTP housing incentive for the following year [S2]
Annual rental reversion on the Jakarta and Surabaya mall portfolio

blocks.text: **BUY — target Rp312, 25.6% total return including the next twelve months' dividend of Rp12 from a Rp258 share price.**

Pakuwon Jati is the wrong kind of property company to value on presales momentum. The recurring portfolio — shopping centres, offices, serviced apartments and hotels — produced IDR5,617.0bn of the group's IDR7,111.1bn revenue in FY2025, against IDR1,494.0bn from development [S5 p.126]. That mix means the earnings base is a rent roll, not a handover schedule, and it is why the audited depreciation charge of IDR764.1bn matters so much (see the financial analysis): the data pack carries about a tenth of it, and every cash-cost comparison built on the pack is therefore wrong [S5 p.343].

The variant view is simple. The market is capitalising the whole group at 5.3x FY2025 earnings, 0.6x book and 4.5x EV/EBITDA, with a 5.0% dividend yield [S0]. Our RNAV values the land at its audited inventory cost and capitalises the rent roll at a secondary-city cap rate; it comes out far above the price. What we will not do is assume the gap closes on its own. The discount we apply is the discount the market applies at the current price, so the RNAV leg's own value prints Rp258 — the share price itself — and the return has to be earned by the roll, the dividend, the growth in the rent roll and the two capped cross-checks.

**What produces the expected return.** Four sourced drivers explain it, and none of them is discount convergence. First, the RNAV leg is held at the 72.1% discount the market applies at the Rp258 price rather than a narrower target: with no dated catalyst inside twelve months and a four-year record of the book multiple de-rating (from 0.6x today against a FY2025 book multiple near three-quarters), assuming convergence would be a wish, not a forecast [S0][S2]. Second, the rolling of that value at the cost of equity over twelve months adds the required return, and the dividend of Rp12 is paid in cash [S6]. Third, the pe cross-check applies our own four-year average multiple of 10.2x to trailing earnings, giving Rp497. Fourth, the pbv cross-check applies 1.0x book, giving Rp489. Weighted at 90.0% RNAV, 5.0% pe and 5.0% pbv, the target is Rp312 and the total return 25.6%. The multiples are deliberately small weights: they use trailing metrics the engine cannot re-price inside a scenario, so they are anchors, not forecasts, and at today's multiples of 5.3x and 0.6x they would print about the share price — the sensitivity a reader should hold beside the headline.

**What today's price implies.** At Rp258 the market is paying 0.6x of book value for a portfolio whose investment properties are carried at depreciated cost, and about 4.5x of EBITDA for a business that converted IDR3,707.9bn of EBITDA in FY2025. Read the other way, the price implies a recurring-asset cap rate far above the one we apply and no value at all for the development pipeline. The reverse-DCF solve cannot bracket the observed price from the operating cash flows we model: our modelled value sits above the price across the whole solve range, which tells us the discount is not a cash-flow question but a willingness-to-pay question — liquidity, index weight and the market's memory of the property down-cycle [S0].

**What moves the value.** The three levers are the discount the market pays for RNAV, the cap rate applied to the recurring base and the recurring margin; presales matter for the timing of development cash, not for the asset value. That is why the scenario table in the risk chapter shocks those three inputs and why the sensitivity grid's presales axis barely moves the target — an honest statement of what this method reads, not a modelling defect [S5].

Indonesian developers have traded at persistently wide discounts to net asset value since the 2013 taper episode, because land is marked at cost, presales are opaque and the rupiah has been volatile. The discount narrows when rates fall and household credit grows, and widens when mortgage rates rise or policy support is withdrawn. This is a structural feature of the asset class, not a comment on any one company.

Pakuwon Jati is an integrated property group whose centre of gravity is recurring income. It owns and operates 11.0 count shopping centres with 859,000 square metres of net leasable area, 6.0 count office buildings with 155,000 square metres of gross floor area, and a hotel portfolio of 2,621 rooms at the end of FY2025 [S5 p.60][S5 p.128]. Around those assets sit two townships covering 1,100 hectares, of which 521.7 hectares remained as land bank at the end of FY2025 [S5 p.61][S5 p.123]. The group is therefore three businesses in one balance sheet: a landlord, a hotel operator and a land developer.

**Segments and mix.** The LK splits revenue into recurring and development. Recurring revenue was IDR5,617.0bn in FY2025 from IDR5,191.0bn in FY2024, covering shopping centres, offices, serviced apartments and hotels [S5 p.126]. Within that, the shopping-centre, office and serviced-apartment block produced IDR4,278.0bn and hospitality produced IDR1,339.0bn in FY2025 [S5 p.122]. Development revenue — landed houses, condominiums and office units sold — was IDR1,494.0bn, up slightly from IDR1,480.0bn in FY2024 [S5 p.126]. The nine-month FY2026 disclosure shows the same shape: retail leasing revenue of IDR3,124.0bn and condominium and office sales of IDR508.0bn against total revenue of IDR5,208.0bn [S2 p.16][S2 p.15].

The implication for the model is direct. Roughly four-fifths of revenue is contracted or quasi-contracted rent and room income, and the remaining fifth is the volatile part. That is why we build the forecast in two blocks, with development revenue driven by presales and a recognition lag, and recurring revenue grown on rental reversion and new hotel capacity [S5 p.126].

**Strategy.** Management's stated strategy is to keep expanding the recurring base while monetising township land at a measured pace. The pipeline named in the LK is the fourth phase of Kota Kasablanka (Eluna Tower), further phases at Pakuwon Mall and Pakuwon City, and hotel additions including Fairfield and Four Points Bekasi and Aloft Pakuwon City [S5 p.40][S5 p.128]. Capital allocation follows the same logic: capex goes into investment property that earns a rent, while development capex is largely funded by presales and the land is already owned. The company's own disclosure of additions to property, equipment and investment properties in FY2025 was IDR485.7bn, a modest share of the operating cash flow the portfolio throws off [S5 p.343].

**Footprint and market position.** The portfolio is concentrated in Greater Jakarta and Surabaya, the two largest and deepest retail markets in the country. Pakuwon is a leader rather than a challenger in that niche: its superblock model — a mall anchored by a township, offices and hotels on the same podium — is hard to replicate because it depends on owning large contiguous land parcels in mature catchments, which the group assembled over decades [S5 p.60]. The land bank is the moat: a competitor can build a mall, but not buy the catchment at cost.

**Group structure and control.** The company is majority-controlled by PT Pakuwon Arthaniaga, which held 68.7% of the shares at the end of FY2025, with the public holding 31.3% and a negligible remainder with affiliated parties [S5 p.18]. Alexander Tedja, the group's founder, is President Commissioner, and the Tedja family is represented on both the board and the management team [S5 p.34]. That concentration is the usual IDX trade-off: strategic continuity and long holding periods on one side, and a minority that cannot change course on the other. The governance chapter treats those consequences properly.

**What the business is not.** It is not a national mass-market housebuilder. Development revenue is small relative to the rent roll, the townships are in two cities rather than twenty, and the company does not chase volume with discounted launches [S5 p.122]. That is a deliberate choice with a valuation consequence: the earnings are higher quality than a pure developer's but the growth rate is lower, which is exactly why we weight RNAV over a growth multiple.

The Indonesian retail property model is built around strata-title sales in some segments and retained ownership in others. Pakuwon's choice to retain its malls — rather than sell strata lots — is what creates the recurring income and the asset backing, but it also ties up capital that a strata seller would recycle. This is a structural difference from several listed peers and explains why the balance sheet, not the income statement, is where the value sits.

**Where we are in the cycle.** Indonesian residential property is in a slow, policy-supported trough. Bank Indonesia held its policy rate at 5.75% at the October 2026 meeting, ending a short easing sequence and signalling that the central bank wants the rupiah to stabilise before it cuts again [S7]. Mortgage rates follow the policy rate with a lag, and housing credit growth has been decelerating: the share of mortgages in total household credit and the run-rate of primary-market house sales both softened through 2026, with developers leaning on incentives rather than price cuts [S10]. That is the macro backdrop against which every listed developer's presales line is being set.

**The house tilt, and why we own it anyway.** The house macro deck carries an AVOID tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive property inside a balance-of-payments-pressure regime, with Bank Indonesia held at 5.75% and the rupiah under pressure [S7, house macro deck]. We do not ignore it. The tilt is why the base case assumes no rate cut, why the RNAV discount is held at 72.1% rather than narrowed, and why the bear case carries 25.0% probability. The argument for a BUY against the tilt is that the tilt is a call on developers whose value waits for a presales recovery and a cheaper mortgage, while this name is valued on assets already owned and income already contracted: the recurring book is IDR5,617.0bn of IDR7,111.1bn revenue, the rent roll covers the notes several times over, and the shares are priced at 0.6x book with a 5.0% dividend yield [S0][S5][S9]. We assume no sector re-rating inside twelve months — the return is the roll at the cost of equity, the dividend and the two capped cross-checks; a rate cut is bull-case upside, not base. If rupiah pressure forces a hike, the bear case is the number that matters, and its intrinsic value of Rp213 sits below today's price rather than at it, so we do not treat the current price as a floor [S7].

**Policy is the swing factor.** The government's value-added-tax incentive for housing (PPN DTP) has been the single most important demand lever for the sector, and its extension is a live policy question rather than a settled one [S2]. When the incentive is in force, the effective cost of a new house falls and developers can hold price; when it lapses, buyers defer and presales fall. Pakuwon's own disclosure ties its development revenue trajectory to the incentive's availability, and the nine-month FY2026 figures show the effect: the IDR508.0bn of condominium and office sales within the nine-month development line (which also carries landed-house sales) and total revenue of IDR5,208.0bn, with presales still short of the prior year [S2 p.15][S2 p.16]. We therefore treat the incentive as a scenario variable, not a base-case assumption: the base case has no extension, the bull case has one.

**The land market.** The only land print in the record is a Jawa Pos survey from October 2023, not a Jakarta-fringe quotation from this year: it puts prime land in South Jakarta and West Surabaya at tens of millions of rupiah per square metre and medium land at a fraction of that [S8]. Set against our carrying value, which implies roughly a million and a half rupiah per square metre across the bank, the gap is very large. We still keep land at cost, for three reasons: a trade-press asking price for small plots in two districts is not an appraisal of several hundred hectares spread over six cities and partly committed to roads, water and recreation; the house card's normal practice is an appraisal less a haircut of a quarter to a half, and we have no appraisal; and a mark-up applied to an asking price would put the RNAV on a comp we cannot verify. We show the direction instead: marking the whole bank at half the low end of the survey's medium range would multiply its carrying value several times and lift RNAV by more than a third, which is why the bull case's asset leg is real. That the base does not pay for it is the largest single criticism of this report, and we state it rather than bury it [S8][S5 p.272].

**Competitive landscape and market share.** The listed peer set is small and each name has a different model: some are mass-market housebuilders with national footprints, some are township developers, and a few are retail landlords with listed vehicles. Pakuwon's differentiation is the superblock — a mall, offices, hotels and a residential catchment on one site [S5 p.60]. That model gives it pricing power in the catchment, cross-traffic between the retail and residential components, and a captive audience for its hotel rooms. It also concentrates exposure: a weak Jakarta or Surabaya retail market hits the same asset twice, through rents and through the value of the surrounding land.

**Five forces.** *Supplier power* is low on the operating side — tenants are fragmented and construction contractors are abundant — but high on the land side, where the holder of a large contiguous parcel has real bargaining power. *Buyer power* is moderate: mall tenants negotiate hard on rent but cannot easily replicate the catchment, and house buyers are price-sensitive and incentive-sensitive. *New entrants* face a high barrier in the superblock model because it requires land, capital and a decade of permits, but a low barrier in plain residential estates. *Substitutes* are meaningful and growing: e-commerce takes retail sales but not necessarily mall visits, and online retail has shifted the tenant mix toward food and beverage and experience, which is where the company has been re-leasing [S5 p.24]. *Rivalry* is moderate in malls — a mall in the same catchment is a zero-sum fight — and intense in mid-market housing.

**Moat assessment.** We score the moat as narrow-to-moderate. The land bank at cost and the location of the malls create a real cost advantage that cannot be competed away quickly; the brand is recognised but not pricing-powerful outside its catchments; and the recurring contracts are short enough that tenants can renegotiate at each renewal. A moat that protects the assets but not the growth rate is exactly the kind of business where net asset value is the right primary method and a growth multiple is the wrong one [S5 p.60].

**External influences to watch.** Three matter for the next twelve months. The rupiah, because a weak currency keeps Bank Indonesia cautious and delays the rate cuts that would compress the discount to RNAV [S7]. The fiscal budget, because the housing incentive is a line item that can be extended or dropped [S2]. And interest rates globally, because the company's dollar notes are a refinancing event in 2028 and the cost of rolling them depends on the offshore market as much as on the company [S5 p.40]. Each of these is a scenario input in the risk chapter, not a hand-wave.

Indonesia's property cycle is unusually policy-dependent by regional standards: mortgage subsidies, VAT incentives and down-payment rules have all been used as counter-cyclical tools, so developers' earnings often reflect the fiscal stance more than underlying household formation. This is why analysts in Jakarta spend more time on budget documents than on site visits.

**Five-year history restated.** The five-year financials the data pack delivers are complete but, in Pakuwon's case, materially incomplete on a key line. The company's FY2025 depreciation and amortisation charge, per the segment note, was IDR764.1bn [S5 p.343]; the data pack carries about a tenth of that. The reason is structural rather than a Yahoo error: the LK presents its cash-flow statement by the direct method, so there is no reconciliation line carrying depreciation for the pack to pick up, and the charge is disclosed in the income statement and the segment note instead [S5 p.343-344]. The same applies to capex: the pack's FY2025 line is well below the LK's total additions of IDR485.7bn, which we now carry as the historical fact [S5 p.343]. We have restated the D&A line as facts F6–F7 and the capex line as F31, and built the historical revenue, cogs, opex and tax from the LK's statements of profit and loss. The restated numbers reproduce the company's reported FY2025 EBITDA of IDR3,707.9bn and net profit of IDR2,346.1bn, and give us the correct base-year cost line for the forecast.

**Revenue build and margin.** Our forecast follows the template two-component logic. Development revenue is driven by presales growth of -17.0% in FY2026E, the recognition ratio of 60.0% and a development gross margin of 54.0% [S5 p.126]. The FY2026E presales decline is our own arithmetic from the reported run-rate, not a company target: marketing sales were IDR811.0bn in the first nine months, a tenth below the same period a year earlier [S4], because roughly half of that volume depended on the PPN DTP incentive [S4]. Carrying that monthly pace through the fourth quarter leaves the full year at -17.0% against FY2025's IDR1,300.0bn, our own arithmetic rather than a company target [S2 p.23]. We do not extrapolate the Q4 seasonal share because we do not assume the incentive is extended. We hold the recognition ratio at 60.0% through the forecast, because the mix stays heavy on landed houses, which are faster to hand over than high-rise condominiums [S5 p.126].

Recurring revenue grows at 7.0% in FY2026E, based on the nine-month run-rate [S2 p.16], eases to 5.0% by FY2030E, and carries a blended gross margin of 56.0%. The mix matters: the retail, office and serviced-apartment block earns a higher segment gross margin than the hotels, and the weighted blend is what we model [S5 p.127-128]. Margins are held flat; we think any rental reversion the Jakarta malls achieve will be offset by wage and utility inflation, and the hotel margin is tied to occupancy more than rates [S5 p.128].

**Cost structure.** SG&A as a share of revenue is 14.1%, the FY2025 actual rather than a three-year average: overhead rose to that level with the new hotel pre-opening and mall marketing spend, and no source supports a saving back to the earlier ratio [S5 p.32]. Holding the actual is also what closes the engine's calibration gap to the last actual year, which is the right test of a cost line. D&A, now restated, is held at the same share of revenue that the restated IDR764.1bn gives. Capex is modelled as 7.5% of revenue, above the FY2025 additions of IDR485.7bn because the pipeline (Pakuwon Mall's next phase, Mall Semarang, the fourth phase of Kota Kasablanka) runs into the high single digits [S5 p.343]. Mall Semarang moved from plan to construction after the balance-sheet date: the group broke ground on 2 November 2026 on a first phase with an investment value of IDR5,600.0bn and a 2029 opening, funded from operating cash flow [S12]. Working‑capital needs are driven by the engine default, which captures the average of the last three years' advanced payments from cash buyers—a key driver of net working capital for a developer with strong presales [S0].

**Cash flow, debt and capital allocation.** The model shows free cash flow rising from IDR2,910.8bn in FY2026E to IDR4,529.9bn in the final year of the explicit forecast, before terminal growth. Two restatement points govern how to read that line. First, the D&A charge of 10.6% of revenue, taken from the LK notes rather than the pack, rebuilds an EBITDA line that explains why the multiple on that EBITDA is so wide [S5 p.343]. Second, the engine's free cash flow is struck as EBIT less the income-tax rate and therefore does not deduct the final tax, which the LK reports as a separate expense line above PBT — IDR434.1bn in FY2025 [S5 p.274, note 29a]. FY2026E free cash flow is therefore before that charge, and the unweighted DCF cross-check it feeds is an upper bound rather than a fair value. The company does pay cash tax on property and rental revenue: the final tax is charged on gross transfers and rentals, so the low reported income-tax rate is a low income-tax position, not a low cash-tax one.

Debt is net‑cash position by FY2030E, driven by the USD note buyback the company undertook in May 2025 [S5 p.40]. Our base case assumes no net new borrowing — the operating surplus finances the upkeep capex — and a cost of debt of 5.5%, the blended rate the company reports on its borrowings [S9 p.28].

Capital allocation is straightforward. The payout ratio is 27.0%, delivering a dividend of Rp12 per share after dividends of IDR626.0bn in FY2025 [S6][S5 p.32]. That ratio is held through the forecast, which means DPS climbs as earnings recover. The company has not raised equity and we assume none; the share count stays at 48,159.6 million shares [S5 p.18].

**Balance‑sheet health.** Net debt is negligible against steady‑state cash flow; interest‑cover from the recurring EBITDA is ample; and the dollar debt is matched by a dollar financial-asset book. At the end of the third quarter the group held total cash and other financial assets of IDR13,508.0bn against gross debt of roughly the 333.4 million dollar notes, of which IDR5,830.0bn is the USD portfolio [S2 p.28]. The hedge is explicit as well as natural: rupiah call spreads cover about four-fifths of the note, struck between fifteen and seventeen and a half thousand rupiah to the dollar [S2 p.28]. The only leverage event is the refinancing of the 2028 notes, which carry a 4.9 per cent coupon and which we assume are rolled at a similar rate once the rupiah stabilises [S5 p.7]. The leverage headroom is one of the reasons we think the stock can absorb rate rises and still support a buy‑back.

**Earnings‑quality flags.** The accruals screen reads the opposite way at a developer with a presales book. We run the three‑year ratio as net profit less operating cash flow over total assets, and at Pakuwon the sign is negative in each of the last three years: buyers pay before handover, so operating cash flow runs ahead of accounting profit and a negative ratio is the healthy reading, not a warning. In FY2025 net profit of IDR2,758.5bn sat below operating cash flow of IDR3,029.0bn on total assets of IDR36,466.0bn; in FY2024 the gap was wider still, with net profit of IDR2,421.7bn against IDR3,354.0bn of operating cash flow on IDR35,371.0bn of assets; and in FY2023 it sat between the two, IDR2,381.9bn against IDR2,734.0bn on IDR32,711.0bn of assets. The trend is therefore a negative gap in all three years, widest in FY2024 and narrowest in FY2025 as handovers caught up with collections — the reverse of the deteriorating conversion a positive accruals build would flag. Receivables growth and inventory growth were broadly in line with revenue growth in FY2025. The restatement of D&A is itself a positive sign: a pack that understates depreciation is not necessarily cooking cash, only reporting on a different basis [S5 p.343][S0].

The IDX special‑monitoring‑board and notation‑letter screen is clean: no flagged board, no negative equity, no opinion modifying phrase in the audit report [S5 p.100]. Dividend payments in cash have been regular, an indirect vote of confidence in the cash‑flow quality [S6][S0].

**Summary.** This is a cash‑generating property portfolio mispriced because the market focuses on the development cycle and forgets about the rental escalators. Disagreements about the intrinsic value revolve around the right cap rate and discount, not around the sustainability of the rent roll. That is exactly the kind of argument you want to have: the downside is anchored by the asset floor (land at cost, malls at a cap rate) and the upside depends on macro and policy decisions you can hedge separately [S5][S0].

**Why RNAV is the right primary method.** A property developer's earnings are a timing artefact: revenue is recognised when a house is handed over, not when the value is created, and the value is created when land is bought and entitlements are won. That mismatch is extreme at Pakuwon, where four-fifths of revenue is rent but the balance sheet holds land bought decades ago at cost. An earnings multiple applied to a handover schedule tells you almost nothing about what the company owns; a net asset value tells you what it owns and lets you argue separately about how much of that value the market will pay for. We therefore weight RNAV at 90.0%, with pe and pbv at 5.0% each as market-anchored cross-checks [S5]. The multiples carry a fraction of the industry default because they are trailing metrics that embed a re-rating to four-year average multiples the RNAV leg deliberately does not assume: at a larger combined weight, part of the target would be invariant to every stress test and would lean the other way from the asset work, which is exactly the defect the reader should not have to find for himself. The weights and the reason are recorded in the assumptions file.

**Cost of capital.** The risk-free rate is the rupiah government curve at 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, the country risk premium is 2.5%, and we relever the industry's unlevered beta of 0.90 at a gross debt-to-market-capitalisation ratio of 0.48 and the statutory tax rate, giving a levered beta of 1.24. The engine's build is *not* the textbook risk-free-plus-beta-times-premia: it deducts the sovereign default spread embedded in the rupiah risk-free rate before adding the levered beta times the sum of the two premia — 7.4% minus 1.6% plus 1.24 times the sum of 4.2% and 2.5% — which is the 14.1% cost of equity used here. Leaving the default-spread term out would reproduce the same inputs as a cost of equity roughly a point and a half higher, and the difference matters because this COE rolls the twelve-month target. The pre-tax cost of debt in the engine is 9.4% — the rupiah risk-free rate plus the corporate default spread, i.e. a marginal rupiah-equivalent cost. That is deliberately not the 5.5% blended rate the company actually pays today [S9 p.28]: the existing dollar coupon is a legacy price and the 2028 notes will be repriced. With weights of 67.5% equity and 32.5% debt, WACC is 11.9%. Two caveats we would rather state than hide: the debt weight is gross, so it ignores the IDR13,508.0bn of cash and financial assets and overstates the group's leverage in both the beta and the WACC; and this WACC feeds only the unweighted DCF cross-check, not the target. On a net basis the company holds net financial assets, which would cut the relevered beta back to the unlevered one and lower the cost of equity by roughly two points — the conservative measure stays, and the reader can see what it costs.

**The RNAV build, line by line.** The cap rate is the largest single judgement in this report, so it goes first. We capitalise the next twelve months of recurring revenue at the segment gross margin of 56.0% and divide by a 10.5% cap rate — property net operating income, struck after property operating costs and before corporate overhead, which is the basis on which market cap rates are quoted. That rate is generous on the harsher test, and we put the number beside the headline rather than in a footnote: measured on EBITDA after corporate overhead, the 56.0% segment margin applied to the next twelve months of rent and room revenue, less the IDR1,010.0bn SG&A line, implies a post-overhead yield of seven and a half per cent, below the eight-to-nine per cent prime range — our own estimate, since no Indonesian cap-rate index sits in the archive. At a genuine eight-and-a-half per cent on that post-overhead base the portfolio would be worth about an eighth less, shaving roughly eighty rupiah a share off the RNAV leg. We keep the NOI basis because property cap rates are quoted on net property income; the reader can price the generosity from those two sentences. The resulting value is nearly three times the IDR12,226.5bn at which the investment properties sit on the LK's balance sheet, so this is a genuine mark-up and not a cost floor.

The other half of the build is the land. We take the LK's real-estate inventory at cost — current and non-current — and treat it as the land and development value, because the company does not disclose a market appraisal of its parcels and an unsourced appraisal is marketing rather than valuation [S5 p.272]. That choice is how we apply the house card's haircut to the land bank: we apply no mark-up at all, so the value is already at the conservative end of the range before any discount. Then subtract net debt and minorities at book, add cash and financial assets of IDR13,508.0bn — a total that now includes the USD portfolio of IDR5,830.0bn held against the 333.4 million of dollar notes, so the hedge is netted against the debt it hedges rather than deducted gross [S2 p.28] — and divide by the share count.

The result before the discount is an RNAV per share well above the current price; after applying the 72.1% discount the market itself applies at today's price, the RNAV method gives Rp258 per share — the share price, by construction. That is the point rather than a defect: we hold today's discount rather than assuming convergence because no dated catalyst falls inside twelve months, and because the shares' own book multiple has de-rated without mean reversion, from about one and a quarter times book in FY2022 to about six tenths today [S0]. A controlling shareholder at 68.7% with no intention of selling, and land carried at cost rather than marked, are the structural reasons a discount exists at all. With the asset leg pinned to the price, the twelve-month return has to come from the roll at the cost of equity, the dividend and the cross-checks below.

**Cross-checks and why they diverge.** The P/E method applies our own four-year average multiple of 10.2x to trailing attributable profit and produces Rp497, which is 92.5% above the RNAV method. The P/BV method applies 1.0x to reported book and produces Rp489, 89.3% above RNAV. The earnings basis is the audited FY2025 profit attributable to owners of IDR2,346.1bn [S5 p.274], keyed from the LK. The data pack's own trailing-twelve-month figure, over the last four reported quarters, runs below the company's trailing profit because its quarterly allocation to minorities is heavier, so the leg reads the audited year rather than importing that error into a 5.0% weight in the target [S0][S2 p.15]. Both legs are trailing, not forecast, and both are fixed when a scenario is run, which is the whole reason they carry only a tenth of the weight between them.

The disclosure that matters is the re-rating these two legs assume, and the sensitivity that goes with it. The shares trade at 5.3x FY2025 earnings and 0.6x book today; the legs apply 10.2x and 1.0x, so they carry a re-rating to the multiples of the four-year window. Held at today's multiples instead, both legs would print about the Rp258 share price, the blend would fall back to the RNAV leg and the target would be the twelve-month roll alone — that is the sensitivity, and it is why the weights are 5.0% each rather than the industry default. Stated plainly: with the asset discount held and no convergence assumed, the target's premium over the twelve-month roll is the multiple gap, and a reader who rejects that gap should read the RNAV leg and the dividend as the valuation. We hold the RNAV discount at today's level for want of a catalyst and, in the same blend, keep a capped weight on multiples from a period when the shares traded at twice today's book: both choices are stated here, and neither is dressed up as conservatism. The divergence is not a modelling error and we do not "fix" it by nudging inputs. A property developer that trades near book and at a low earnings multiple will always screen cheap on relative value and expensive on asset value; the weighted target splits the difference at Rp312, and the 25.6% total return clears the house bar by a thin margin. We would rather name that than pad it: strip the two cross-checks out and the RNAV leg at today's discount returns only the cost of equity plus the dividend, so the part of the call that is not the roll is the multiple gap — the shares trading at half their four-year average book and near half their average earnings multiple — and we have capped the weight at which that view can be expressed.

Two caveats on scope, and they run in opposite directions. The RNAV values the development pipeline at land cost, so Eluna Tower and the township phases are worth their sunk land and nothing more until they produce cash flow — a deduction, since a buyer would pay something for the entitlement. Against it, the land is at cost when the only market print in the record suggests replacement cost is far higher (see the industry chapter). Neither caveat changes the rating, and neither is dressed up as a margin of safety in the other direction.

**Sensitivity.** The target moves with the RNAV discount and the cap rate, and barely at all with presales. That is not a defect we can engineer away: an asset-based method does not read a marketing-sales number, and the two earnings multiples are trailing and fixed inside the grid. We show the presales axis anyway, because it is the KPI the company reports monthly and the one a reader will reach for, and we say plainly that its effect on this valuation is close to nil. What the presales path does move is the cash that funds the dividend and the credibility of the earnings cross-checks. The discount is the single most important variable in the target, and it is the variable a catalyst would move; the cap rate is the second, and because the 10.5% NOI rate is equivalent to seven and a half per cent after corporate overhead, the cap-rate axis should be read as the generosity test on the whole RNAV rather than as a market print we have observed.

**What today's price implies.** We tried to solve the reverse DCF — hold the model, ask what price the cash flows justify — and it does not bracket the observed price. The engine returns no implied value because the modelled value exceeds the price across the whole solve range. That is not a reason to ignore the exercise; it is the finding. At Rp258, the market sits at the RNAV leg's post-discount value of Rp258, which is to say the 72.1% discount we hold is the discount the market is already applying: the price embeds no convergence and no value for the development pipeline, and our operating model says the cash flows are worth more than that. That points to something outside the cash flows: the market's required return on Indonesian property equity, the liquidity of the shares, or simply the memory of the last down-cycle. The practical conclusion is that the re-rating has to be catalyst-led, because the arithmetic is already on our side.

Indonesian developers rarely trade at parity with net asset value even in good years; a discount of several tens of per cent is the norm, and the discount compresses most reliably when Bank Indonesia is cutting rates and mortgage growth is accelerating. That is why the scenario design in this report shocks the discount to RNAV as well as the operating drivers — in this sector the multiple and the fundamentals are two separate bets.

**Downside risks and likelihood.** Five categories: *Regulatory*: the value-added-tax incentive for housing is regularly acted by parliament; its lapse or redesign could cut presales materially without a price cut, as buyers defer. Likelihood moderate–high, impact moderate (the development segment is a minority of revenue). Company disclosure notes the incentive's importance [S2]. *Macro*: Bank Indonesia stays hawkish longer than expected, keeping mortgage rates above price-sensitive thresholds and delaying any discount-to-NAV compression. Likelihood moderate, impact moderate to large because the discount, not the cash flow, is the main value lever [S7]. *Currency*: the rupiah weakens further from its Q3 2026 level. The notes are fixed-rate, so this does not raise the coupon; it raises the rupiah carrying amount of the dollar debt and, at the 2028 refinancing, the cost of rolling it. The USD portfolio of IDR5,830.0bn is held against the 333.4 million of notes, so most of the exposure is hedged on the balance sheet [S2 p.28]. Likelihood low–moderate, impact small. *Operational*: the mall portfolio occupancy dips (the office occupancy is already 74.0%, fine but not stellar) or renewal spreads tighten as e‑commerce reshapes tenant demand — a multi-year bleed versus a one‑year spike [S5 p.60]. *Governance*: the company keeps returning cash to shareholders as dividends while the land bank sits idle, or pushes up development margins by shifting the mix toward condominiums with a higher replacement cost later. Likelihood low–moderate, impact moderate (dividend record suggests no risk of abrupt change) [S6].

Two further risks are real but are not shocked, and we say why rather than leave them out. A wider refinancing spread on the 2028 notes raises interest cost, which the RNAV does not capitalise — it is a cash-flow item that shows up in earnings and in the dividend cover, not in asset value; the cost of debt in the model is already a marginal rate rather than today's legacy coupon, so part of it is priced. A fall in development margins hits the handover profit and therefore the earnings cross-checks, but the RNAV values the pipeline at land cost and capitalises no development profit at all, so shocking a margin that the primary method ignores would be theatre. Both would change the bear case's earnings, not its asset value.

**Scenarios.** The house model assigns a base‑case probability of 50.0%, with the tails at 25.0% each. We weight the base at one half because the last actual year's economics are reproducible at today's prices and the company's own disclosure supports the recurring run-rate [S2], not because we are neutral about the outcome.

The three cases shock the same three drivers by mirrored amounts, so neither tail is a story with a number attached. The bear widens the cap rate by fifty basis points, cuts the recurring gross margin by two hundred, and widens the RNAV discount by seven points — rates staying high, occupancy and renewal spreads softening, the PPN DTP lapsing, and the 2028 notes rolling into a wider spread. Presales are not shocked in either tail, because the asset-based method barely reads them and a shock there would be inert: we say so rather than let the table imply a stress it does not deliver. Bear intrinsic value is Rp213 and the bear target is Rp231.

The base case is the primary valuation: presales of -17.0% in FY2026E before recovering, the 72.1% discount, and the recurring growth documented in the industry chapter [S2][S5]. Intrinsic value Rp282, target Rp309.

The bull mirrors the bear — cap rate fifty basis points tighter, recurring margin two hundred basis points better, discount seven points narrower — on a PPN DTP extension and a BI easing cycle, with a buyer marking the malls at a prime rate. Intrinsic value Rp359, target Rp397.

**Signposts that change the view.** We would move to a SELL or a more bearish scenario if, in order of descending confidence: - the PPN DTP incentive lapses and presales drop more than our bear forecast assumes; - Bank Indonesia hikes rates rather than holds to defend the rupiah, pushing mortgage rates above the level at which price-sensitive buyers defer; or - rental spreads on mall renewals deteriorate across the portfolio more than the annual CPI‑plus the company has historically achieved. Conversely, a catalyst that narrows the discount — a rate cut, a large handover, an announcement of a mall sale‑leaseback — lifts the target without changing the cash flows.

What the table says, stated plainly: the bear intrinsic value is Rp213, below the Rp258 price, and the bear target is Rp231 — a negative return, not a floor. We do not dress the current price as downside protection, because the bear widens the discount and a further de-rating is possible; and we equally do not claim the bull, which needs a policy event we do not forecast. The point is that the cash flows and the asset value are not what is being questioned at this price. The discount is — and on our numbers the market is already at the wide end of it.

**Ownership and control.** PT Pakuwon Arthaniaga held 68.7% of the shares at the end of FY2025, the public held 31.3% with no single holder above five per cent, and the remainder sits with affiliated parties including the founder [S5 p.18]. Control is therefore absolute in practice: a minority cannot block a related‑party transaction, cannot force a strategic review, and cannot change the dividend policy. The offsetting fact is that the controlling family's wealth is overwhelmingly in the same shares, which aligns it with the minority on the things that matter most — dividend continuity and asset value.

**Board and management.** Alexander Tedja, the founder, is President Commissioner; the board also includes an independent commissioner and family and management representatives [S5 p.34]. The board has the usual IDX composition rather than an international one: a majority of commissioners are not independent, and the audit committee draws from the independent commissioner role. That is a structural weakness for a minority investor, but it is the norm for family‑controlled Indonesian developers rather than a company‑specific red flag.

**Related parties.** The FY2025 accounts quantify the flow, and it is small: the related-party note tabulates transactions and the only amount disclosed is short-term benefits to commissioners and directors of IDR72.2bn, about one per cent of group revenue of IDR7,111.1bn, with no revenue or purchase transactions with related parties recognised [S5 p.343, note 32]. The note states that transactions were carried out on arm's-length terms and that no conflict-of-interest transaction was entered into during the year [S5 p.144-145], and the accounting policy confirms the group does not grant loans to related parties outside ordinary trade terms [S5 p.287]. That is a clean screen on the modal IDX value-destruction channel — related-party flow is about a fifth of one per cent of assets rather than the double-digit share that has destroyed value elsewhere — and it is a sourced clean screen, not an absence of evidence.

**Structure flags.** We found no disclosure of pledged shares against the controlling stake, no serial rights issues (the company has not raised equity), and no beneficial-ownership opacity beyond the ordinary. There is no special-monitoring-board status and no notation letter [S5 p.100]. Auditor continuity is intact: the FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Liana Ramon Xenia & Rekan, a member of the Deloitte network, appointed at the June 2025 shareholders' meeting [S5 p.100]. One legal-probe line belongs in the list even though it is not company-level: in August 2026 the KPK examined a Pakuwon Jati general-affairs employee as a witness in the Lamongan regency building case, a project tendered in the 2017-2019 budget years with an estimated state loss of IDR35.7bn [S11]. The company is not a defendant and the employee is a witness, and the contract pre-dates the current development pipeline, so we record it rather than treat it as a structure flag; it would become one if a current director or the company itself were named.

**Dividend record.** The company paid a dividend of Rp13 per share in respect of FY2025, IDR626.0bn in total, a payout of 27.0% [S6][S5 p.32]. The record shows DPS held steady through the downturn rather than cut, which we read as a signal about the board's confidence in the rent roll.

**ESG exposures.** The material issues are physical climate risk (flooding in Jakarta and Surabaya, which the company manages through site drainage and elevated podiums), energy intensity of the mall portfolio, and labour standards in construction contracting. The company discloses sustainability initiatives but not a full scope‑three emissions inventory [S5]. For a long‑held asset base, the largest ESG risk is transition capex on the malls rather than a near‑term earnings hit.

Family control is the default ownership model for Indonesian property companies. It gives long holding periods and stable strategy, and it also gives minority investors a governance discount that shows up in the RNAV discount. The question for an analyst is not whether the family controls the company — it does — but whether the family's interests and the minority's coincide on cash returns. Dividend continuity is the cleanest observable test.

**Dated catalysts.** The calendar that matters over the next twelve to eighteen months is short and specific. *Fourth‑quarter and full‑year marketing sales (early 2027).* Nine‑month marketing sales were IDR811.0bn, down on the prior year, so the fourth quarter will show whether the run‑rate holds and whether the PPN DTP incentive was extended [S4][S2]. *The FY2026 results (March 2027).* The key lines are recurring revenue growth (we model 7.0%), the recurring gross margin, and the two tax lines: the income-tax rate is unusually low because the final tax on property and rental revenue sits separately above PBT [S5 p.274]. *Eluna Tower handovers (from 2029).* The Kota Kasablanka phase‑four tower is the next large development recognition event and the first test of the high‑rise margin, but it is outside the twelve‑month window, which is why it does not support a shorter discount [S2 p.23]. *Annual rental reversion (ongoing, reported with the results).* The reversion rate on mall renewals is the single best indicator of whether the rent roll can grow faster than inflation [S5]. *The 2028 notes refinancing (approaching).* A successful roll at or below the existing coupon would remove the last balance‑sheet question [S5 p.7][S9 p.28].

**KPIs we monitor.** Marketing sales and the presales‑to‑revenue recognition ratio; mall occupancy and the reversion rate; retail NLA and the count of malls and hotels (the quantities we track through 11.0 count, 859,000 square metres and 2,621 rooms) [S5 p.60][S5 p.128]; office occupancy, currently 74.0% [S5 p.60]; recurring revenue growth and segment gross margin; net debt and the USD financial‑asset offset; and the dividend per share and payout [S6].

**What would make us wrong.** We would revisit the rating if the recurring revenue run‑rate stalled for two consecutive periods, if the office occupancy fell materially from its current level, if a related‑party transaction of a size that changes the equity story appeared, or if the discount to RNAV narrowed to the point where the target return no longer justified the position. On the other side, evidence that the company can recycle land into cash faster than we model — a township land sale, a strata disposal, a joint venture with an institutional partner — would raise the RNAV and bring the bull case closer [S2].
